name: ForkUnion
workload: N-body dispatch latency (N=512 bodies, every logical core) and 84-round connected-components label propagation (27M edges) measuring fork-join dispatch cost.
claimed_speedup: README headline: ~3-6x faster than OpenMP and ~12-16x faster than Rayon and Taskflow per parallel-for dispatch. N-body on 128x Intel SPR Linux, static/dynamic us: ForkUnion C++ 54/86, OpenMP 115/226, Rayon 483/739, Taskflow 666/694. Connected components GTEPS: ForkUnion C++ 46.5/20.9, OpenMP 28.2/0.4, Rayon 8.5/6.5, Taskflow 25.1/0.5.
compiler_and_flags: -O3 -march=native (C++), RUSTFLAGS target-cpu=native for Rust, no LTO; parity enforced across runtimes, stated in README footnote
hardware: Machines named by core count and generation only (18x Apple M5 Pro, 24x Intel RPL Windows, 128x Intel SPR Linux, 192x AWS Graviton 5); exact CPU models not given
tradeoffs: Fork-join parallel-for only: no task graphs, futures, async I/O or nested parallelism (deliberately banned). NUMA-aware, no hot-path allocation/syscalls/CAS. Bindings for C, Rust, Zig.
caveats: First-party benchmark by the author; benchmark code is public (scripts/nbody.cpp, propagation.cpp) but CPU models are not exact, so not tier A. OpenMP and Taskflow are not the TBB baseline; oneTBB is not measured. Gaps are on dispatch-bound loops; on bandwidth-bound loops on M5 Pro and RPL OpenMP is close or ahead (e.g. 11.4 vs 10.0 GTEPS static on 24x RPL).
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'C++ parallel_for library faster than OpenMP thread pool low latency fork-join'; README read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: citor
baseline: Intel oneTBB (also OpenMP, Taskflow, dispenso, BS::thread_pool, Eigen::ThreadPool, libfork)
workload: Independent tzcnt/runtime-benchmarks recursive fork-join suite: skynet (100M tasks), nqueens, fib(39), matmul(2048) on 64 threads; plus the project's own dispatch, reduce, scan and forkJoin benchmark suite.
claimed_speedup: runtime-benchmarks 64-core EPYC 7742: mean ratio to best 1.06x for citor vs 3.25x oneTBB, 3.34x Taskflow, 1.18x libfork. fib(39) 49966 us vs oneTBB 215592 us; skynet 24932 us vs oneTBB 142887 us; nqueens 80765 us vs oneTBB 125730 us (libfork 69010 us is faster there). Own README: wins the vast majority of contested cells on a single Zen 5 CCD against oneTBB, OpenMP, Taskflow, dispenso.
hardware: EPYC 7742 64-core, 64 worker threads, no SMT, Debian 13 (runtime-benchmarks); own bench on Zen 5 9950X3D single CCD, AWS c7a.metal-48xl and c7i.metal-24xl
tradeoffs: Header-only C++20, Linux x86_64 and Windows; latency claims validated on Linux only. Tuned for single-CCD Zen with core pinning; per-CCD arenas needed on multi-CCD servers.
caveats: Suite is maintained by the TooManyCooks author (a competitor), but code is public. README admits losses: barrier-bound stencils lose to OpenMP on multi-CCD, heavy-tailed reductions lose to oneTBB (static partitioning), and win rate is lower on Genoa and Sapphire Rapids. citor memory use is higher (nqueens 51 MB vs oneTBB 12.7 MB). Numbers read from the README table via raw.githubusercontent.com.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'github C++ coroutine task scheduler work stealing benchmark vs TBB Taskflow'; tzcnt/runtime-benchmarks README

name: inkooboo/thread-pool-cpp
claimed_speedup: Reposting 1,000,001 jobs in about 61-70 ms vs about 1,380-1,390 ms for the asio-based pool (about 20x).
tradeoffs: Header-only C++11; work-stealing and work-distribution modes; MPMC bounded queue. Fixed-size task wrapper.
caveats: Not compared against TBB, OpenMP or Rayon; baseline is an asio pool (incumbent but outside the category list). README gives no compiler, flags or CPU. LICENSE note: the MPMCBoundedQueue part is under separate terms (hence mixed). Last commit date not confirmed. The yvoinov/thread-pool-cpp fork reports the same numbers.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'C++ work stealing thread pool faster than TBB OpenMP benchmark github'
